interviewQuestions.question: What is training-serving skew, and how do feature stores prevent it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd define it concretely: training-serving skew happens when the feature values a model learned from during training are computed by a different pipeline — often different code, a different language, a different team — than the feature values it receives at serving time in production, and those two pipelines disagree on some edge case even though they're meant to compute "the same" feature. A real example: training computes "days since last login" in a batch Python job with one timezone convention and null-handling rule, while serving computes it in a separate low-latency Java service with a subtly different rule — both look correct in isolation, but the model now sees systematically different inputs live than it learned from, degrading accuracy with zero errors thrown anywhere. Feature stores prevent this structurally: a feature is defined **once**, in one place, and both the offline store (used to build training datasets) and the online store (used for low-latency serving) are populated from that single shared definition — there's no second, independently-written implementation left to drift out of sync. They also add point-in-time correct joins for training data (so you don't accidentally leak future feature values into historical training rows) and feature versioning (so a live model keeps getting the exact feature version it was trained on, even as the definition evolves elsewhere).

**Testing:** whether you understand skew as a dual-implementation problem specifically, and can name the structural fix (shared definition) rather than a vague "consistency between training and serving" answer.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Dual implementations as the root cause

interviewQuestions.question: Your team built a training dataset by joining historical labels to the current feature values in your feature store, rather than the values as of each label's timestamp. What's the risk, and how would this actually show up?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
This is future leakage through a point-in-time join done wrong, and it's a specifically dangerous bug because it produces training data that's subtly invalid rather than obviously broken — the pipeline runs successfully, produces a normal-looking dataset, and the model trains without any error. The core problem: a label from six months ago represents a decision that had to be made using only the feature values that existed *at that time* — if you instead join it to the feature's current value, and that feature is something that accumulates over time (a customer's total lifetime purchases, total support tickets, account age), the "current" value already includes information from *after* the label's timestamp — information the model wouldn't have had access to at real prediction time.

Concretely, this would show up as a model that looks excellent offline but underperforms in production in a way that's hard to pin down initially: a churn model trained this way might learn that "high total lifetime purchases" strongly predicts "didn't churn" — but a meaningful chunk of that correlation could be circular, since customers who didn't churn six months ago obviously went on to make more purchases in the following months, and that later purchase history leaked into their "total" feature value even though it postdates the churn label. The offline evaluation looks great because the same leakage is present in the held-out test set too — it's not caught by a normal train/test split, since the leak is a property of how each row was constructed, present in every row equally.

The fix is enforcing genuine point-in-time joins — every feature value used for a given label must be the value that existed at or before that label's timestamp, never after — which is exactly the specific correctness guarantee feature stores are built to automate, since doing this manually and correctly across many features and models is notoriously easy to get subtly wrong.

**Testing:** whether you can trace the specific mechanism by which future leakage inflates offline metrics without being caught by a normal test split.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Diagnosing future leakage from a bad point-in-time join

interviewQuestions.question: A startup with three models and one small ML team is debating whether to adopt a full feature-store platform like Feast or Tecton right now. How would you advise them?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd push back on adopting the full platform immediately, and recommend starting with a lighter-weight solution: a well-governed shared table or view that both training and serving genuinely read from, rather than standing up new infrastructure and a new team skill set before there's a demonstrated need for it. A full feature-store platform earns its cost — built-in point-in-time joins, online/offline consistency guarantees, cross-team feature governance and versioning — specifically when you have enough models and teams that manual point-in-time correctness and feature reuse across teams become a real, recurring, expensive problem. At three models and one small team, that governance and reuse problem mostly doesn't exist yet — feature definitions can be coordinated informally, and the setup and operational cost of a new platform is a real tax without much benefit to offset it yet.

The minimum I'd still insist on regardless of scale: whatever training and serving each read from must be the *same* shared table or definition, not two independently maintained implementations — that structural discipline is what actually prevents training-serving skew, and it's achievable cheaply even without a dedicated platform. I'd also flag that if their training data construction involves joining historical labels to feature values, they need to get point-in-time correctness right manually, and that manual correctness is exactly the part that becomes error-prone as complexity grows — so I'd revisit this decision explicitly once they're adding, say, a fifth or sixth model, hiring a second ML team, or hitting a genuine low-latency serving requirement a shared table can't satisfy.

**Testing:** whether you can give a cost-aware recommendation calibrated to actual scale, rather than defaulting to "always adopt the more sophisticated tooling."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Right-sizing feature-store adoption for a small team
